summary: Early mathematical modelling for ages 5-6: children use objects, drawings, or dictated/written number sentences to REPRESENT a real situation, and then read an answer back off the model as something about the real objects. The whole modelling cycle appears in miniature: the model must preserve what actually happens in the story (a taking-away action, not just the numbers 5 and 2), and the answer must be interpreted in context ('three apples left', not a bare 'three'). The central hazard to head off is 'suspension of sense-making' — computing without checking the story — addressed by habitually asking 'does your model match what happened?' and 'three what?'. Teaching is concrete, story-driven, and two-way (situation→model and model→story).
misconceptions: Models the numbers but not the action — draws 5 and 2 as if adding when the story takes away
Gives a bare number ('three') without saying what it means about the apples
Accepts an answer that contradicts the story (more apples after eating some) — doesn't check the model against the situation
Draws the objects decoratively without preserving the quantities in the story

activities.title: Act the story on cubes, then read the answer back
steps: Listen to or watch a short story, e.g. 'I had 5 apples in a bowl and I ate 2 of them'
Show the story with counters/cubes: start with five, then physically remove two to model the eating as a taking-away
Optionally arrange the counters on a five-frame or ten-frame to structure and see the quantities clearly
As the model settles on three, say or build the matching number sentence 5 − 2 = 3
Answer the question 'three what?' by saying 'three apples left' and pointing to the three remaining in the model
Check the model against the story: 'Does what I did to the cubes match what happened to the apples?'
activities.insight: The model must preserve the ACTION of the story (taking away), not just the numbers; and the answer is three apples still in the bowl, not the bare number 3.

activities.title: Work both directions: invent a story from a model
steps: Receive a model, e.g. a bowl that started at five and now holds three cubes
Decide what could have happened and tell the story aloud: 'I ate two apples'
Build or dictate the matching number sentence (5 − 2 = 3) for the story you invented
Explain what each part of the model stands for in your story
activities.insight: A model carries the whole situation — action and all — both ways: a story can be turned into a model, and a model can be read back as a story.

activities.title: Puppet tells a story and sometimes gets it wrong
steps: Listen to a puppet tell a story and ask you to show it with objects or a drawing
Build the model and say what the answer means ('three apples left')
Catch the puppet when it models the story wrongly, e.g. 'I had 5 apples and I ate 2, so now I have 7?' — explain why that can't be right
Tell the puppet your own story for a model it shows you
activities.insight: Telling a matching story and interpreting what the answer means is a two-way, sense-making conversation; an answer that contradicts the story (more apples after eating some) must be rejected.

activities.title: Diagnostic: does the friend's drawing match the story?
steps: Hear the story: 'I had 5 apples and I ate 2 of them'
Look at a friend's drawing that shows 5 apples and then 2 MORE apples drawn next to them
Decide whether the friend's drawing matches the story, and explain why or why not
Show how YOU would represent the story, modelling the eating as removal
Say what your answer means about the apples ('three apples left')
activities.insight: A child who models the situation catches that the friend drew a joining (adding) when the story takes away, and interprets the answer in terms of apples; attending only to the numbers (there is a 5 and a 2) misses the mismatch.

checkQuestion: Here's my story: I had 5 apples and I ate 2 of them. A friend drew 5 apples and then drew 2 more apples next to them. Does my friend's drawing match my story? Show me how YOU would show my story, and tell me what your answer means about the apples.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child noticing the friend's drawing ADDS (5 and 2 more) instead of taking away, modelling the eating as removal, and reading the answer back as 'three apples left', not a bare 'three'.
